consensus_summary: Primary figurative sense is distant Gentile nations or remote coastlands that await and receive God’s law and salvation; secondary apocalyptic sense is islands as stable elements or powers removed under judgment.
book_summary: A set-apart sanctified covenant people—the rock/mountain risen out of the sea of nations—waiting for the law that sanctifies it, the ‘island of the innocent’ delivered to safety while the kingdoms fall.
book_core_identification: set-apart sanctified covenant people (rock risen out of the sea of nations)
boundary_disagreement: Book reassigns the Isaiah ‘isles that wait for his law’ and remnant recovery from islands to the sanctified covenant people rather than Gentile nations, and reads the flight of islands in Revelation as deliverance of the innocent rather than removal in judgment.
material_contradiction: Consensus core equates islands with (or as metonym for) the distant Gentile nations themselves; book equates islands with a people set apart and risen out of those nations (the sea). The two cannot both be the primary symbolic referent.
rationale: All four consensus responses identify the dominant figurative meaning as distant Gentile nations/coastlands (Isaiah, Psalms, etc.) with apocalyptic removal as a common secondary stream and isolation or church-as-island as rare. The book replaces that central referent with the sanctified covenant people as a rock emerging from the sea of nations, folding in Job 22:30 and a deliverance reading of Rev 16:20. The rare ‘church amid sea’ alternative covers only a fragment and is not the consensus core; the identifications therefore contradict rather than refine a shared category.
strongest_objection: Standard interpretation of the Hebrew ʾiyyîm treats it as geographic metonymy for distant Gentile nations, not a typological symbol for a set-apart covenant people; Job 22:30’s ‘island of the innocent’ is a contested KJV rendering often revised, and Revelation’s fleeing islands are uniformly read as judgmental upheaval.
